title: Let the Interface Tell the Truth When the System Is Struggling
summary: Slow, partial, stale or uncertain: how to show real system limits on screen, what the backend must track to do it, and how to word the message so users trust it.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The screen looks fine. The Submit button is there as usual, the dashboard has its friendly layout, the empty state looks patient. Meanwhile the logs know the queue is backing up, the payment provider is answering in eight seconds instead of one and the next export will take five times longer than normal. The user is about to find out the hard way.

We usually talk about architecture behind the screen: queues, retries, rate limits, storage pressure, a slow vendor, a fallback path. Users only meet it through the screen. If the screen acts like every path is always available, the system can be technically correct and still mislead the person using it. This post is about closing that gap: which limits to show, what the backend needs so you can show them, and how to word it.

An old rule with numbers attached

"Visibility of system status" is the first of Jakob Nielsen's usability heuristics: the design should keep users informed about what's going on, with feedback within a reasonable time (NN/g). Nielsen also put rough numbers on "reasonable" back in 1993. About 0.1 second feels instant. About 1 second keeps the user's flow of thought. About 10 seconds is the limit for keeping their attention, and past that people start doing something else while they wait (Response Times: The 3 Important Limits).

NN/g's progress indicator guidance turns that into a design rule: show something for anything longer than about a second, use a looping spinner for roughly 2 to 10 seconds and a percent-done indicator for 10 seconds or more (Progress Indicators Make a Slow System Less Insufferable). The same article cites a University of Nebraska–Lincoln study where people who saw a looped progress bar were willing to wait about three times longer than people who saw nothing.

These numbers are useful for engineers because they tell you which operations need a different contract. If an action can take 40 seconds when a vendor is slow, a spinner on a synchronous request is the wrong design, not just the wrong animation.

Polite lies, and what to say instead

Most dishonest interfaces aren't malicious. They're tidy. Somebody chose the clean version of the screen, and the mess moved to the user and the support team.

Polite lieHonest version
A spinner with no end, on an export that takes ten minutes"Big report, usually about 10 minutes. You can leave this page; we'll email you the file."
"Payment successful" before the provider has confirmed"We've got your payment request. The bank is slow right now. Don't pay again; this page updates when it's confirmed."
A disabled button with no reasonThe button stays disabled, with one line underneath: "You've hit today's limit of 20 exports. It resets at midnight UTC."
A dashboard that hides how old its data is"Data as of 09:15. Next refresh is running."
Search results that look complete while the index rebuilds"Some recent items may be missing while we update search."

None of the honest versions explain the machinery. Nobody needs to hear that partition two is slow. They need the part of the limit that changes their next decision: wait, leave, don't retry, come back later.

You can only show what the backend tracks

Here's the part that makes this an architecture topic. "Data as of 09:15" needs a freshness timestamp. "Don't pay again" needs an idempotent payment request (more on that in Designing APIs That Survive the Second Click). "We'll email you" needs the work to live in a job with a status, not inside an HTTP request that the browser might drop.

For long work, Microsoft's Asynchronous Request-Reply pattern is a good default (Azure Architecture Center). The API checks the request, answers right away with 202 Accepted, and points the client at a status endpoint:

HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
Location: /exports/exp_8f2c/status
Retry-After: 10

Location says where to poll and Retry-After says roughly when. The status endpoint returns 200 with the current state while the work runs, then redirects with 303 to the result when it's done. The pattern suggests a documented set of states (pending, running, succeeded, failed, canceled) plus timestamps so a client can tell a stalled job from a slow one. Add a freshness field and you have everything the screen needs:

{
  "status": "running",
  "createdAt": "2026-11-17T09:02:11Z",
  "lastUpdatedAt": "2026-11-17T09:04:40Z",
  "percentComplete": 40,
  "dataAsOf": "2026-11-17T09:00:00Z"
}

Each field maps to a line of UI copy. percentComplete drives the progress bar that NN/g recommends past 10 seconds. lastUpdatedAt lets the screen say "still working" honestly, or switch to "this is taking longer than expected" when nothing has moved for a while. dataAsOf is the "as of 09:15". Also decide early which failures are temporary, which are final and which need a human, because the screen will need a different sentence for each.

When the limit is a rate limit, the same idea applies to the 429 response. Rate Limiting and Throttling Without Punishing Real Users covers how to word it.

Different people need different depths

One system, several honest stories, none of them contradicting each other:

  • The user needs the effect on their next step: delayed, partial, stale, don't retry.
  • Support needs the request ID, the status history and the time of the last change, so they can answer "is it stuck?" without paging an engineer.
  • The on-call engineer needs the queue depth, the vendor latency and the trace. That's what observability as a design choice is for.

A good test: if support and the user look at the same job at the same moment, do their two screens tell the same story at different depths?

How to word it

People forgive a system that says it's slow far more readily than one that looks confident while failing. The message doesn't need drama. Four parts cover almost every case: what happened to their request, what's going on (in their terms), what they should or shouldn't do, and when they'll hear next. "We received your request. Processing is slower than usual. You don't need to resubmit. This page will update when it's done."

Honest screens look a bit less polished in the design review, because limits are messy. Hiding the mess doesn't remove it. It just moves it to a support ticket, a duplicate payment or a user who stopped trusting the button. A limit you name on screen becomes part of the contract. A hidden one turns up later as a surprise, usually at the worst moment.

Try this week

  • Pick one flow and mark every step that can be slow, partial, stale or uncertain.
  • For each mark, write the one sentence the screen should say at that moment.
  • Check whether the backend tracks what that sentence needs: a status, a timestamp, an idempotency key.
  • Find one spinner on an operation that can take more than 10 seconds and give it a real status instead.
  • Add a "data as of" time to one dashboard.

faqs.q: What does it mean for an interface to be honest about system limits?
faqs.a: It tells users the part of a limit that affects their next decision: that an action is delayed, partial, based on stale data or uncertain, and whether they should wait, retry or come back later. It doesn't expose internal details like which partition is slow.

faqs.q: When should I use a spinner versus a progress bar?
faqs.a: Nielsen Norman Group recommends showing an indicator for anything longer than about one second, a looping spinner for roughly 2 to 10 seconds and a percent-done indicator for 10 seconds or more. If an operation can take much longer than that, move it to a background job with a status the user can check.

faqs.q: How should an API handle long-running requests so the UI can show progress?
faqs.a: Use the Asynchronous Request-Reply pattern: validate the request, return 202 Accepted with a Location header for a status endpoint and a Retry-After hint, then report a documented status, timestamps and optional percent complete until the work finishes and the endpoint redirects to the result.
